inline.s: [Unable to give rise to right faith in a single thought] Here 'a single thought' means having no other thought at all. [Jue] Its.

[Recalling the karma of my past rebirths, I cannot know for how many thousands of kalpas. Following darkness, entering the Unintermittent [hell], undergoing all kinds of suffering, I cannot know how long. And when I sought the Buddha Way, not encountering a good friend, I sank for long kalpas, in darkness without awareness, committing all kinds of evil karma. At times when I think of this, I cannot help a long sigh. How could I slow down and again receive those past misfortunes? And who knows who will again cause me now to encounter a human life, to be the spirit of all things, and not lose the path of true cultivation? Truly this is the blind turtle meeting a plank of wood, a tiny blade of grass thrown to pass through a needle's eye; how could one exhaust words for such good fortune!]

Recalling the karma of my own past rebirths, I cannot know for how many thousands of great kalpas. Sinking in darkness, entering the Unintermittent hell, undergoing all kinds of suffering, I cannot know how long! And when I sought the Buddha Way, I did not meet a good friend, and so sank for long kalpas, in darkness without awareness, committing all kinds of evil karma. When these circumstances are brought to mind, I cannot help a deep sigh! How could I slow down my practice and again receive those past misfortunes? And who knows who will again cause me to encounter a human life, to be the spirit of all things, and not lose the path of true cultivation? In truth, such an opportunity is like a blind turtle passing through the hole of a plank, or a tiny blade of grass passing through the eye of a needle. And I have this opportunity; how fortunate! How fortunate it is!

[A blind turtle meeting a plank] This is to show how extremely rare the opportunity of temporarily obtaining a human body is. The Buddha told a simile: suppose the whole earth became a great ocean, and there was a blind turtle whose lifespan was measureless kalpas, which surfaced its head only once every hundred years. And on the ocean there was a plank with a single hole in it, drifting everywhere with the wind and waves. The blind turtle surfaces only once in a hundred years; for it to meet this plank is already a slim chance, and how much more so to thrust its head through the hole in the plank? And the chance for living beings to temporarily obtain a human body is harder still than this. [A tiny blade of grass thrown to pass through a needle's eye] Throwing an extremely fine blade of grass and having it pass through the eye of a needle; this too is a simile for the difficulty of temporarily obtaining a human body.
Jie: a small grass.

[If I now give rise to shrinking and dejection, or give rise to sloth, and always look forward to a later time, then the moment I lose my life and fall back into the evil realms, and undergo all kinds of pain and suffering, although I would wish to hear a single phrase of the Buddha Dharma, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, hoping to escape the bitterness, how could I obtain it again? And when one comes to the brink of danger, regret avails nothing!]

If I now give rise to shrinking and dejection, or give rise to sloth, and always think it can be spoken of later, then the moment I lose my life and fall back into the evil realms, and undergo all kinds of pain and suffering, although I would wish to hear a single phrase of the Buddha Dharma, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, to escape the bitterness, how could I? And when one is gravely ill and near death, then to repent is of no use!

[I pray that those who cultivate the Way give rise to no heedlessness, cling to no greed or lust, but, like one who saves his head from burning, never forget to take care. Impermanence is swift; the body is like the morning dew, the life like the western light [of the setting sun]; though you live today, tomorrow is hard to be sure of; take heed! Take heed! Moreover, relying on the worldly conditioned good, one can still escape the wheel of suffering of the three evil paths, and in the heavens and among humans obtain excellent retributions and enjoy all kinds of pleasures; how much more so this supreme and profound Dharma gate, wherein a temporary arising of faith produces merit and virtue that cannot be expressed by parable even in its smallest fraction.]
I pray that those who cultivate the Way,
do not give way to indulgence and pleasure,

do not be greedy for wealth or lustful for beauty, but, urgent as one who puts out a fire on his own head, practice thought after thought, never forgetting to take care of the practice. Impermanence is swift; the body is like the morning dew, and the life like the setting sun. Though you live today, tomorrow is hard to be sure of; take heed! Take heed! Moreover, relying on the worldly conditioned good, one can still escape the wheel of suffering of the three evil paths, and in the heavens and among humans obtain excellent retributions and enjoy all kinds of pleasures; how much more so this supreme and profound Dharma gate, wherein a temporary arising of faith produces merit and virtue that cannot be expressed by parable even for a fraction of it.

[Heedlessness] Giving way to indulgence and pleasure. [Greed and lust] Greed for wealth and lust for beauty. [Never forget to take care] In facing realms and meeting conditions, one must always take care of the practice and not let it be lost. [The wheel of suffering] Because the bitter fruits of birth-and-death turn round and round without stopping, it is called a wheel.

[As the sutra says: 'If a person with the seven treasures of the three thousand great thousand worlds gives gifts and offerings and saturates the living beings of that many worlds, and further teaches all the living beings of that many worlds so that they attain the four fruits, his merit and virtue is measureless and boundless; yet it is not equal to the merit and virtue obtained by, in the time of one meal, properly reflecting on this Dharma.' From this one knows that this Dharma gate of mine is most honored and most noble; compared with all other merits and virtues it cannot be matched. Therefore the sutra says: 'A single thought of pure mind is the place of awakening, surpassing the building of a stupa of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the stupa after all crumbles into dust, while a single thought of pure mind attains right awakening.']

As the sutra says: 'If a person with the seven treasures of the three thousand great thousand worlds gives gifts and saturates the living beings of that many worlds, and further teaches all the living beings of that many worlds so that they attain the fruit of arhatship, then such measureless, boundless merit and virtue is not equal to the merit and virtue obtained by, in the time of one meal, properly reflecting on this Dharma.' From this I know that this Dharma gate of mine is most honored and most noble, and all other merits are far inferior to it. Therefore the sutra says: 'A single thought of pure mind (a single unified thought) is the place of awakening, surpassing the building of a stupa of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, because the stupa after all will crumble into dust, while a single thought of pure mind (a single unified thought) will attain right awakening.'

[I pray that those who cultivate the Way meditate on and savor these words, and surely take heed. If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life will it be delivered? If one does not cultivate now, he will miss it for ten thousand kalpas; if now one strongly cultivates the difficult-to-cultivate practice, it gradually becomes not difficult, and the merit and practice advance of themselves.]

I pray that those who cultivate the Way finely meditate on and savor these words, and surely take heed. If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life will it be delivered? If one does not cultivate now, he will suffer misfortune for ten thousand kalpas; if now one applies effort and strongly cultivates the difficult-to-cultivate practice, it gradually becomes deeper and is no longer difficult, and the merit and practice advance of themselves.

[Alas! The people of today, hungry, meet the king's meal, yet do not know to put it in their mouths; ill, meet the king of physicians, yet do not know to take the medicine. When one does not say 'what is to be done, what is to be done,' there is nothing I can do with him! Moreover, the conditioned affairs of the world have forms that can be seen and merits that can be verified; when a man achieves one thing, people sigh at its rarity. But this mind school of mine has no form to contemplate and no shape to be seen; the path of speech is cut off, and the place of the mind's activity is extinguished. Therefore heavenly demons and outsider paths have no gate by which to slander it, and Shakra, Brahma, and the various devas cannot praise it fully; how much less can those of common, shallow understanding so much as approximate it?]

How lamentable! The people of today, hungry, meet the imperial meal, yet do not know to put it in their mouths; ill, meet the king of physicians, yet do not know to take the medicine. Truly one does not know what to say, what to say! Moreover, the conditioned affairs of the world have forms that can be seen and merits that can be verified; when a person succeeds in a single undertaking, people sigh at its rarity. But this mind school of mine has no form to contemplate and no shape to be seen; the path of speech is cut off, and the place of the mind's activity is extinguished. Therefore heavenly demons and outsider paths have no gate to slander it, and the devas of Shakra, Brahma, and the various heavens cannot praise it fully; how much less could the various words of common, shallow understanding so much as resemble it?

[The mind school] An abbreviation of the Buddha-mind school, that is, the Chan school. [The path of speech is cut off, the place of the mind's activity is extinguished] The ultimate truth is not something that words can speak, nor can the thinking mind imagine or investigate it.

[How sad! How could a frog in a well know the vastness of the great ocean? How could a wild fox produce the lion's roar? Therefore know that one who, in the Latter Dharma age, hears this Dharma gate, gives rise to a thought of its rarity, and believes, understands, receives, and upholds it, has already for measureless kalpas served and attended the sages, planted all kinds of good roots, and deeply formed the right cause of prajna, and is of the highest faculties. Therefore the Diamond Sutra says: 'Whoever can give rise to faith in these verses and phrases should know that he has already planted all kinds of good roots under measureless Buddhas.' And it says: 'It is spoken for those who give rise to the Great Vehicle, and for those who give rise to the supreme vehicle.']

How sad! How could a frog at the bottom of a well know the vastness of the great ocean? How could a wild fox produce the lion's roar? Therefore know that one who, in the Latter Dharma age, hears this Dharma gate, gives rise to a thought of its rarity and believes, understands, receives, and upholds it, has already for measureless kalpas served the sages, planted all kinds of good roots, and deeply formed the right cause of prajna, and is of the highest faculties. Therefore the Diamond Sutra says: 'Whoever can give rise to faith in these verses and phrases should know that he has already planted all kinds of good roots under measureless Buddhas.' And it says: '(This sutra) is spoken for those who give rise to the Great Vehicle, and for those who give rise to the supreme vehicle.'

[Wild fox] A kind of fox; a metaphor for one whose cultivation has not yet matured but who recklessly speaks the truth. [The lion's roar] When the Buddha speaks the Dharma, without any fear, his voice shakes the ten directions and all the demons are subdued, just as when a lion roars all the beasts submit.

[I pray that those who seek the Way give rise to no timidity and weakness, but must rouse a bold and mighty mind. The good causes of past kalpas are not knowable. If one does not believe in the excellence of his own fortune and is content to be low and inferior, giving rise to thoughts of hardship and obstruction, and does not cultivate now, then even though he has good roots from past lives, because he now cuts them off, the difficulty increases all the more and he turns further and further away.]

I pray that those who seek the Way give rise to no timidity and cowardice, but must rouse a bold and mighty mind. The good causes of past kalpas are not knowable. If one does not believe that one's own karmic conditions are excellent and is content to be low and inferior, giving rise to thoughts of hardship and peril, and does not cultivate now, then even though he has good roots from past lives, because he now cuts them off, and so fearing the difficulty of the journey he stops and does not advance, he turns further and further away from the bodhi path.

[The good causes of past kalpas are not knowable] How do you know that you are not of the superior faculties with deep merit and fortune? It is like a gifted boxer who, instead of training hard himself, blames his lack of talent and always loses. [Mi] The same in meaning as 'still' or 'cease,' meaning to stop.

[Now that you have reached the treasure place, you must not return empty-handed; once you lose a human body, it is hard to regain it in ten thousand kalpas. I beg you to be careful! How could there be a wise person who, knowing the treasure place, does not seek it but forever laments his solitude and poverty? If you wish to gain the treasure, put down the leather bag!]

Now that you have reached the treasure place, you must not return empty-handed; once you lose a human body, it is hard to regain it even in ten thousand kalpas. I beg you, do take heed! How could there be a wise person who, knowing the treasure place, does not go to fetch the treasure but forever laments his solitude and poverty? If you wish to gain the treasure, put down this leather bag (the body)!

The sentence 'If you wish to gain the treasure, put down the leather bag' is of the utmost importance. Otherwise, one is holding the post and rowing the boat, and nothing whatsoever is accomplished. Elder Master Xuyun said: 'This body of ours, when the breath no longer comes, is just a corpse. The reason we cannot put it down is only that we value it so, and then arise the distinctions of self and other, right and wrong, love and hate, grasping and rejecting. If you determine that this body is just a corpse, do not treasure it, and utterly do not regard it as myself, then what is there you cannot put down?' Therefore, as long as you put down this leather bag, the mind will of itself not become attached and defiled, all dharmas will not be received, and what undertaking will not be accomplished?
